meta_title: Roadmap · What we build and how to help
meta_description: Every OpenDrone project with its current status: what is nearly in the shop, what is in development, and the pre-design ideas anyone can help shape on Discord and GitHub.
title: What we're building, and how you can help.
lead: OpenDrone is a community project, but that doesn't mean compromise. The end goal is to cover each corner of the FPV hardware spectrum. The way we get there is by first laying out foundational hardware and then building on top of that. We think foundational hardware means all the parts to build a 5 inch or 3 inch freestyle drone, so that roughly translates to: stack (FC + ESC), receiver, frame, motors and video system. You'll find the status of those products below. The ecosystem around the drone is the next part: chargers, accessories, propellers, batteries, consumables, buzzers, GPS. After that, expanding into different size classes like whoops and toothpicks with AIOs, or bigger cinelifters. Step by step, we hope to provide everything you need to build and fly your drone.
s1_body: Everything starts as a conversation on [the OpenDrone Discord](@discord): what the market needs, which specs make sense, what can realistically be produced. Agreeing before anyone draws is the point. It stops two people building the same thing, and it kills bad ideas before someone spends weeks on a layout.

Anyone can propose future hardware. A proposal names an owner who carries the design through review and measurement, and decisions are argued on published measurements, not preference. Products marked **Concept** in the shop are published before hardware exists, precisely so this discussion can happen in public, on Discord.

Incutec, the company behind this shop, supports and steers the development. Contributors whose hardware is verified by the community receive manufactured samples of their own design. Once hardware is verified we can move to small test runs and integrate it in the rest of the OpenDrone ecosystem.
s2_body: The same board we work from. Each product carries exactly one status flag, explained below. The flag is the status: the same value is set as a status-* topic on the product's GitHub repo, and nothing describes status in prose anywhere else.
status_launched_legend: In the shop and settled. The design has stopped moving; buy it and it will not change under you.
status_beta_legend: Launched, first production batch. You can buy it in the shop, early-batch pricing can be lower, and the design can still get updates between batches.
status_alpha_legend: Coming soon. Testing inside the project: community testers and firmware maintainers fly the hardware before anyone can buy it. Where a product page exists, you can join the waitlist there.
status_in-progress_legend: A first design exists and prototypes may already be ordered, but nothing is under test yet.
status_planned_legend: No design yet, on purpose. We name it early so the community can shape the spec from day one: the discussion runs on Discord, and design proposals are welcome. No product listing until there is hardware.
votes_body: Every order carries an optional ballot: rank up to three of the in-progress and planned projects from your cart, and checkout files it with the order. This is how the queue below the betas gets its order. The vote steers our prioritisation; engineering reality can still overrule it, in the open.
votes_empty: No ballots counted yet. Voting ships with the shop: when you order, the cart carries a ranked ballot for what we should build next.
votes_method: Ranked choice: 3 points for a first pick, 2 for a second, 1 for a third.
goals_body: Shop profit goes to R&D and manufacturing, and we would rather show that than say it. So here is what we are saving for, one goal at a time. The meter is computed from sales on a weekly rhythm, in coarse 5% steps: deliberately approximate, never a live feed of our books.
goals_foot: Goals are ours, not earmarks. No order is tied to a machine, and nothing here is crowdfunding; it is just where the margin goes.
s4_body: Flew it, bench-tested it, or just read the schematic and found something off: open an issue on the board's repo. A photo, a log file, or a net name is enough. Confirmed design problems get fixed in the next revision and credited on the product page, receipts linked.
s5_body: Hardware is not software: two people can edit the same code file, but a PCB layout cannot be merged. So each board has one maintainer who holds the layout, and edits are serialised through file locks. Schematics are split across hierarchical sheets, so separate sheets can have separate owners. Two people can hold two boards. Two people cannot hold one layout.

Everyone else contributes through review, and review is where the real capacity is: CI renders the schematic, the board images, ERC and DRC output and a BOM diff on every pull request, so a design one person draws can be reviewed by anyone, without opening KiCad. Small, focused changes land fastest: one connector, one footprint, one silkscreen fix, agreed with the board's maintainer.

Merged design changes show up in the “You asked. We changed it.” chapter of the product page, and your account lands in its contributor grid. Every product page names who developed the board, maintainer first, the way a record sleeve names the band. A handle and avatar are enough; nobody needs your real name.
s6_body: The boards run community firmware: Betaflight, AM32 and ExpressLRS. Work there helps every board, not just ours; €1 of every board sold already goes to these projects. Start with the [firmware partners](/firmware-partners) page if you want the details.
s7_body: Every entry above links to its source where one is public. The hardware is KiCad, latest stable release, licensed CERN-OHL-S v2: strong reciprocal, share your changes. By opening a PR you license your contribution under the repo's license. No CLA, no paperwork.
